narrative:
The model estimates a 54% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability tips above 50%, the system recommends denying your promotion to reduce the risk of investing in someone likely to depart soon.

Three factors drove this prediction, ranked by importance. First, your total years of experience across all jobs (1–5 years) was the strongest influence and pulled the decision toward staying. Most employees the model expects to remain also fall in this early-career range, so the system sees your limited overall experience as a reason you might still build loyalty here. 

Second, having received other job offers while employed here pushed the prediction toward leaving. This signal of external opportunities was the largest factor increasing the likelihood you will exit.

Third, working in the “other” sector (rather than medical or education, where most stayers are concentrated) added a moderate push toward leaving. The model has learned that people in less common sectors tend to change jobs more frequently.

Taken together, the external opportunities and sector effects outweighed the stabilizing influence of your early-career stage, producing the 54% probability.

The organization should discuss with you whether those outside offers can be matched or whether clearer growth paths would increase your commitment. You, in turn, may want to reflect on what would make staying feel more secure and satisfying. Addressing these points openly could change the outlook for both sides.
